paras: The attempted lynching of Chastine Barker was a threatened mob killing at Liberty, Virginia, around February 1, 1888, in which neighbors tried to lynch a white man arrested for assaulting a seven-year-old white girl. Officers held the crowd off with great difficulty, and Barker was lodged in jail. The episode reached southern papers through a single wire dispatch from Lynchburg.

Barker was described as a white man over fifty years old with a wife and grown children. According to a special from Liberty to the Advance, he was arrested on February 1, charged with assaulting "a little white girl aged 7 years."

News of the accusation left "the people in the neighborhood" terribly incensed, and they moved to lynch him. The officers who held Barker had "great difficulty" keeping the crowd from him, but they succeeded. The dispatch gives no size for the crowd and names none of its members.
Barker was held in jail when the report was sent. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict on the assault charge was found, and no one in the crowd is reported to have been arrested.

The story ran on February 2, 1888, in Florida and Georgia papers as a brief wire item datelined Lynchburg, February 1. The Palatka Daily News headed it "Another Brute," presenting the accusation against Barker as settled. The Savannah Morning News ran the same text under "People Thirsty for Gore," with a deck reading "An Old Man Criminally Assaults a 7-Year-Old Girl." Both papers stressed that the accused and the girl were white, and neither commented on the crowd beyond the Savannah headline's reference to its thirst for "gore."
No Black-press coverage is available for this period, and no follow-up in the white press was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Chastine Barker
bases: Both reports say officers had great difficulty keeping incensed neighbors from lynching Barker after his arrest, a threatened lynching of a man in custody (A1, A2).

Barker was not killed: officers kept the incensed people of the neighborhood from lynching him and he was in jail (A1, A2). The crowd's size is not given, but its aim was punishment for an alleged assault on a child.
Both articles relay the same Liberty special to the Advance by wire, so they are one report, not independent confirmation (A1, A2).
